blocks.content: An operating system can feel like a single mysterious thing, but it is really built in layers, stacked from the bare hardware at the bottom up to the apps you use at the top. Each layer has a clear job and talks mainly to the layer just below it.

Understanding this layered picture makes everything else about operating systems click. You can see where your program sits, where the kernel sits, and how a simple action like reading a file travels all the way down to the disk and back.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308464-570833378.png
1. The Layered View

The cleanest way to picture an operating system is as a stack of layers. At the very bottom is the hardware. At the very top are the applications you run. Between them sit the kernel, the system call interface, and system libraries, each bridging the gap.

The rule of the stack is that higher layers rely on lower ones, and lower layers hide their complexity from above. Your app does not worry about disk sectors, it just calls a library, which calls the kernel, which drives the hardware.

blocks.title: A simple picture
blocks.content: Think of a building. Residents on the top floors, the applications, never deal with the foundation and plumbing, the hardware. Floors of staff in between, the kernel and libraries, handle all of that so life upstairs stays simple.
2. Hardware at the Bottom

At the base of everything is the physical hardware: the processor, the memory, the disk, the network card, and all the other devices. On its own, this hardware is just electronics that can do nothing useful without software to direct it.

Every layer above ultimately exists to manage and share this hardware. The whole point of the operating system is to sit on top of the raw hardware and turn it into something programs can use safely and easily.

["The processor, memory, storage, and devices","Raw and powerful, but useless without software to control it","Shared among many programs by the layers above","Everything higher up exists to manage this hardware"]

Raw and powerful, but useless without software to control it

Everything higher up exists to manage this hardware

blocks.content: 3. The Kernel: The Core Layer
Directly above the hardware sits the kernel, the core of the operating system. The kernel is the only software that talks to the hardware directly, and it runs with full privileges in kernel space.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308464-9638471.png

Inside the kernel live the components that manage each resource: a scheduler that decides which program runs on the processor, a memory manager that hands out memory, a file system that organises storage, and device drivers that speak to hardware.

["The core layer, running with full privileges in kernel space","The only software that touches the hardware directly","Contains the scheduler, memory manager, and file system","Uses device drivers to communicate with each device"]
items: The core layer, running with full privileges in kernel space
The only software that touches the hardware directly
Contains the scheduler, memory manager, and file system
Uses device drivers to communicate with each device

blocks.title: The kernel is small on purpose
blocks.content: Because kernel code is trusted with the whole machine, operating systems try to keep it focused. Everything that does not truly need full privileges is pushed up into the layers above.
4. The System Call Interface
Between the kernel and everything above it sits the system call interface. This is the boundary that separates the privileged kernel from the restricted programs, and the only doorway through it.

When a program needs the kernel to do something, it makes a system call, which crosses this interface into kernel mode. The interface defines exactly which requests are allowed, so the kernel controls precisely how the outside world can reach it.

["The boundary between user space and kernel space","The only controlled way for programs to reach the kernel","Defines the set of requests programs are allowed to make","Every privileged action passes through this interface"]
items: The boundary between user space and kernel space
The only controlled way for programs to reach the kernel
Defines the set of requests programs are allowed to make
Every privileged action passes through this interface

blocks.title: The guarded gate
blocks.content: The system call interface is the single gate in the wall around the kernel. Programs can pass through it, but only in the exact ways the kernel permits, which is what keeps the system secure.
5. System Libraries
Above the system call interface sit the system libraries. These are collections of ready made code, running in user space, that programs use so they do not have to make raw system calls themselves.

The C standard library is the classic example. When you call a function like printf or fopen, you are using a library that packages up the messy details and, when needed, makes the underlying system calls for you. Libraries make programming far easier and more portable.

["Reusable code that runs in user space","Wrap raw system calls in friendly, convenient functions","The C standard library is the classic example","Make programs easier to write and more portable across systems"]

Wrap raw system calls in friendly, convenient functions
The C standard library is the classic example
Make programs easier to write and more portable across systems

blocks.content: 6. Applications and the Shell
At the top of the stack are the user applications: your browser, your editor, your games, and the programs you write. They rely on everything below to actually get anything done.

The shell is a special application worth naming. It is the command line interface that lets you type commands to run programs, and it was one of the original ways people interacted with an operating system. Graphical desktops are the modern equivalent, another top layer application through which you drive the system.

["User applications sit at the very top of the stack","They use libraries and system calls to reach the kernel","The shell is the command line application for running programs","A graphical desktop is the modern top layer interface"]

blocks.content: 7. Kernel Designs
Not all kernels are built the same way. The big architectural choice is how much to put inside the kernel versus how much to keep outside it, and this gives rise to two main designs.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308465-51426365.png

A monolithic kernel puts most services, including drivers and file systems, together in kernel space. This is fast, because those parts can call each other directly, but a bug in any of them can crash the whole system. Linux is the famous example.

A microkernel keeps only the bare minimum in kernel space and runs services like drivers as separate user space processes. This is more robust, since a crashing driver does not take down the kernel, but it is slower because those parts must communicate through messages. Many systems use a hybrid that blends both.

8. How a Request Flows
The layered picture comes alive when you trace a single action through it. Consider a program reading a file.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308465-918395149.png

["The application calls a read function","That goes into a system library, which prepares a system call","The system call crosses the interface into the kernel","The kernel and the disk driver fetch the data from the hardware","The data travels back up the layers to the application"]
items: The application calls a read function
That goes into a system library, which prepares a system call
The system call crosses the interface into the kernel
The kernel and the disk driver fetch the data from the hardware
The data travels back up the layers to the application

blocks.content: Every layer does its part and hands off to the next. The application never touches the disk, the library never touches the hardware, and only the kernel driver actually speaks to the device. That clean handoff, layer by layer, is the whole architecture working as designed.
9. Why Layering Matters
The layered design is not just tidy, it delivers real benefits that make modern computing possible.

["Simplicity: each layer has one job and hides its complexity from above","Security: the kernel boundary keeps programs from harming the system","Portability: apps written to the libraries work across different hardware","Maintainability: a layer can change internally without breaking the others"]
items: Simplicity: each layer has one job and hides its complexity from above
Security: the kernel boundary keeps programs from harming the system
Portability: apps written to the libraries work across different hardware
Maintainability: a layer can change internally without breaking the others

blocks.content: Portability is a quiet but huge win. Because your program talks to libraries and system calls rather than the hardware, the same program can run on very different machines, as long as the layers below present the same interface. The operating system absorbs the differences.

blocks.title: Layers hide differences
blocks.content: The reason the same app can run on wildly different hardware is that each layer hides the details below it. The application sees a clean, stable interface, and the messy variation is handled underneath.
